body.text: PNG to sell Australian-funded electricity infrastructure worth millions
In short:
Papua New Guinea will sell off power stations that received millions of dollars in upgrades funded by Australia.
Six stations were earmarked for $25 million in Australian funding for upgrades, with work completed on two.
PNG says the stations are placing "financial pressure" on the government.
Papua New Guinea is selling off millions of dollars' worth of Australian-funded electricity infrastructure, including newly built solar power plants, the ABC has confirmed.
The regional assets are managed by state-owned PNG Power, which has faced allegations of corruption, mismanagement and unstable leadership over several years.

PNG Prime Minister James Marape announced earlier this month that the 18 power centres across the country would be sold via an open tender, arguing the centres were putting "financial pressure" on the government.
Six of the centres up for sale were chosen to receive a $25 million upgrade in 2021 from an Australian-funded program called the PNG Electrification Partnership.
The Australian-funded work has been completed at Aitape, and work has started at Kimbe and Buka.
Australia also helped fund a solar power station at Arawa, the ABC has confirmed.

In announcing the sale, Mr Marape said the decision followed a comprehensive assessment of the power centres' financial performance, which found they were costing the government about 54.1 million kina ($17 million) annually.
In 2024, Mr Marape announced the partial privatisation of PNG Power, with the company trying to claw its way out of extraordinary debt.
The ABC recently revealed PNG Power owed more than $1.5 billion to creditors and was insolvent.
Australian-funded solar power station first in PNG
Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs declined to say how much had been spent on the power stations.
PNG ministers have said the Aitape solar farm cost 16.6 million kina ($6.3 million).

Previously, the Australian High Commission announced the first stage of a solar power upgrade project had been completed at Arawa in Bougainville in 2024, with two further stages due to be completed in 2025.
In 2022, Australia funded two new generators at Daru in the Torres Strait at a cost of about $1.2 million, according to a High Commission statement at the time.
The statement said the work was the first stage of the Australian government's commitment to upgrade and transition the Daru electricity grid to renewable energy.

As recently as November 18, the High Commission said Australia was supporting upgrades to the Kimbe electricity grid, that site preparation was complete, and construction was underway on a new solar and battery storage project.
Construction was due to be completed in 2027.
Aerial photos posted by the High Commission show a significant area has already been cleared for the solar facility at Kimbe.
PNG's sell-off attracts criticism and questions
Former PNG prime minister Peter O'Neill has criticised the sell-off and said the government should prioritise settling its outstanding electricity bills.

"They should immediately pay the outstanding K200 million ($67 million) plus power bill … so that it can relieve the cash flow issues that PNG Power is facing before any issue about privatisation is considered," Mr O'Neill said.
He called for a commission of inquiry into the cash-strapped energy behemoth, saying it was failing the people of PNG.
"There are constant blackouts right throughout the country," he said.

Paul Barker, who heads the independent Australian policy think tank the Institute of National Affairs, said the main concern with privatisation was ensuring reliable and affordable electricity supply.
"Who is going to manage these sort of off-grid systems anyway?"
Mr Barker said.
"There are not going to be many entities that are going to be willing to put their hands up."

He said provincial governments or local entities would most likely consider taking over the assets, but the possibility of a foreign government or state-owned company also coming in could not be ruled out.
Both PNG Power and Mr Marape's office did not respond to the ABC's questions.
Minister backs in government's handling
The minister responsible for state-owned enterprises, William Duma, has defended the government's handling of PNG Power, despite the enterprise being moved out of his portfolio earlier this year.
Mr Marape said the decision to sell the plants followed a comprehensive assessment of the centres' financial performance and the business case for divestment.

He said an assessment by advisory firm KordaMentha found the small centres generated negative earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of approximately 54.1 million kina ($18 million).
"Without reform, they will continue to place financial pressure on PNG Power and consume resources that could otherwise be directed towards improving electricity services," he said.
"Cabinet has chosen an open and competitive tender rather than direct or negotiated sales to ensure transparency, accountability and the best possible value for public assets."
Mr Marape has said that provincial governments would be given the first chance to take part through joint ventures with trusted private investors.
In 2024, the PNG government rejected media reports it was considering selling PNG Power to China and that management from the company had travelled to China for meetings.
The sell-off comes as the Australian government has committed $290 million to help fund a PNG Rugby League franchise.
